newsitem.title: USA: CBO sees Clinton budget at deficit in year 2002.
newsitem.headline: CBO sees Clinton budget at deficit in year 2002.

text.p: Congressional Budget Office Director June O'Neill said Thursday that President Clinton's five-year budget proposal would yield a $50 billion deficit in the year 2002, not the $17 billion surplus the White House forecast.

O'Neill told the House Budget Committee she expected interest payments on the federal debt and spending for entitlement programs such as Social Security to be higher in the coming five years than the White House assumed.

O'Neill repeated the caution she had issued in testimony before Senate budget policymakers last month in which she warned that arranging to balance the budget by 2002 may be more difficult this year than last year.
She added that the problem will get only worse because of the impact on government spending of the retirement of the baby boom generation and continuing growth in health care costs after 2007.

"Taking action now would contribute to ensuring budgetary stability in the next century," she said, adding that the most benefits would be seen if the government dealt with the problems of federal health care and other retirement benefits.
"Doing so would make the additional policy changes required in the future much less painful," she said in testimony prepared for delivery before the House panel.
O'Neill repeated the agency's earlier forecast for the U.S. economy, which she said was very close to the blue chip consensus for the next two years.
"CBO sees no dark clouds on the horizon," she said.
CBO projected U.S. economic growth at 2.2 percent in 1997 and 1998. It said inflation and interest rates were expected to remain near current levels.
For the long term, CBO sees moderate growth and continued low inflation.
O'Neill warned that a recession late in the year 2000 could add another $100 billion to the projected deficit for 2002. However, CBO has not forecast such an economic downturn.
O'Neill questioned the effectiveness of Clinton's proposal to automatically cancel tax cuts and reduce spending, if necessary, to end the deficit in 2002.
